questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify an example of distributive policy
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-101 asks the team to identify which of the city's programmes is a straightforward example of distributive policy.

options.text: Repairing the carriageways on the routes that carry the heaviest traffic each year.
Charging higher rates for water use in blocks where consumption is above the national average.
options.misconception: confuses a regressive charge with a distributive benefit

options.text: Setting minimum safety standards for scaffolding erected on commercial building sites.
options.misconception: treats a regulatory standard as a distributive transfer

options.text: Funding a subsidised bus pass for every resident over the age of sixty-five.
options.misconception: mistakes a targeted subsidy for a general allocation

questions.explanation: Distributive policy allocates benefits across the population, and road repair on a published route list does that. The distractors confuse it with charges, standards and targeted subsidies.
questions.hint: Ask whether the programme hands out a benefit.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a targeted grant is redistributive policy
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-104 asks the team to explain why a grant that lowers rates in the poorest wards counts as redistributive policy.

options.text: Because it hands out money directly to residents through unconditional cash transfers.
options.misconception: confuses reallocation with a direct cash transfer

options.text: Because it makes the city's overall spending on services larger than it was before.
options.misconception: assumes redistribution means spending more overall

options.text: Because it shifts resources from a shared pool towards groups that receive less of it.
Because it concentrates spending in one area rather than spreading it thinly everywhere.
options.misconception: treats concentration of spending as redistribution

questions.explanation: Redistribution moves resources towards those who receive fewer of them. The distractors substitute a cash transfer, a bigger total budget and geographic concentration for a change in who gets what.
questions.hint: Ask who gains at whose expense.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the inspection capacity of a regulatory unit
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-107 asks the team to work out how many food premises a two-officer regulatory unit can inspect in a week if each inspection takes two and a half hours and each officer has thirty hours of field time.
questions.explanation: Two officers supply sixty hours, and at two and a half hours per inspection that allows twenty-four premises. The tempting error divides one officer's hours by the inspection time.
questions.hint: Add the officers' time before dividing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select a framing that opens a policy window
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-112 asks the team to judge which framing of a housing issue is most likely to open an agenda window.

options.text: Frames the issue as a shortage of construction workers in the building trades.
options.misconception: assumes supply-side framings always open windows

options.text: Frames the issue as a matter of local heritage rules restricting new building.
options.misconception: assumes procedural objections attract political attention

options.text: Frames the issue as a failure by developers to meet their own affordable housing quotas.
options.misconception: blames one sector where the responsibility is diffuse

options.text: Frames the issue as a shortage of homes, a condition that touches most voters directly.

questions.explanation: Agendas open when a problem is framed so that it connects to widely shared concerns. The distractors use blame narratives or technical framings that narrow the constituency for action.
questions.hint: Ask which framing touches the widest constituency.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a policy window opened from council minutes

stimulus.body: An item on homelessness funding was listed in the forward plan three times without debate, then reached full council in March, the month after a national newspaper ran a series on shelter costs. A motion to widen the item was defeated by a procedural vote, and a revised version was tabled the following month with a budget figure attached.

questions.stem: Memo PLAN-115 asks the team to identify what the minutes suggest about the timing of the policy window.

options.text: The window closed early, because the item failed to secure a procedural vote in March.
options.misconception: reads one procedural defeat as a closed window

options.text: The window opened in March, because the newspaper coverage forced the item onto the agenda.
options.misconception: assumes coverage alone determines the agenda

options.text: The window was already open, because the item had appeared three times in the forward plan.
options.misconception: confuses listing in a plan with a real window

options.text: The window opened around March, and the procedural vote suggests it was narrow and contested.

questions.explanation: A window opens when attention and readiness coincide, and a narrow procedural defeat fits a contested opening. The distractors treat one defeat as final and credit coverage alone.
questions.hint: Consider attention, readiness and the reaction.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish programme outputs from outcomes
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-119 reports that a homelessness team built 180 beds and served 1,200 households while the citywide number of rough sleepers fell by 9 per cent, and asks the team to interpret this.

options.text: The bed and casework figures are outputs, while the rough sleeper count is closer to the outcome sought.
The fall of nine per cent shows the programme produced a large improvement in homelessness.
options.misconception: treats a trend as proof of programme impact

options.text: The outputs exceed the outcome, so the programme is performing below expectation.
options.misconception: compares delivered activity with measured outcome

options.text: The team should be judged on beds built, because outcomes here are too easily manipulated.
options.misconception: asserts outputs are safer because outcomes gameable

questions.explanation: Outputs are what a programme delivers; outcomes are the change it seeks. The distractors read a trend as causal, compare unlike measures, and use gameability to justify counting activities.
questions.hint: Ask what changes if the programme stops.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a policy operates without a controlling authority
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-123 asks the team to explain how a waste collection policy is often implemented without going through the council.

options.text: The council delegates the contract to a contractor, which then decides the collection rounds itself.
options.misconception: assumes a contractor's discretion equals a subgovernment

options.text: The council applies a statutory standard that the collection crews already meet voluntarily.
options.misconception: treats compliance with a standard as a policy web

options.text: A network of contractors, crews and regulators acts together, and none of them controls the others.
The national ministry sets the collection rounds, and the council simply records them.
options.misconception: assumes a single authority runs implementation

questions.explanation: A policy subgovernment is a web of actors with a shared interest, sustaining a policy without one controlling authority. The distractors reduce it to delegation or voluntary compliance.
questions.hint: Ask who would have to agree for it to stop.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State what distinguishes corporatist consultation
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-128 asks the team to state what distinguishes corporatist consultation from an open public hearing.

options.text: It gives every resident the same length of time to speak before the committee.
options.misconception: assumes consultation is universal in reach

options.text: It gives designated organised bodies privileged access to shape the proposal before the hearing.
It requires the committee to publish every submission it receives in full.
options.misconception: confuses transparency with privileged access

options.text: It requires a minimum number of public comments before the committee may vote.
options.misconception: reads a procedural rule as the purpose of consultation

questions.explanation: Corporatism gives recognised groups a structured, privileged role in shaping policy. The distractors replace that with equal individual access, publication rules and a procedural trigger.
questions.hint: Ask who is guaranteed a seat at the table.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Account for why a discretionary favour was expedited
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-132 asks the team to account for why a councillor's office was willing to expedite a permit for a supporter.

answer.exemplar: The willingness to expedite a permit is best explained as a personal exchange, in which the councillor trades a discretionary favour for political support rather than applying a published rule that anyone could invoke. Such behaviour survives when the benefits are small, hard to monitor and easy to deliver informally, and when the recipients are politically useful, because the individual gain is immediate while the cost is spread thinly across every resident who waits. A defensible account therefore combines the incentive structure of discretionary powers with the weakness of oversight, and distinguishes the exchange from ordinary constituency casework where a published service standard governs the outcome regardless of who asks.

questions.explanation: Clientelism links a discretionary favour to political support, and it flourishes where rules are opaque and oversight weak. The tempting account of routine casework ignores the personal exchange.
questions.hint: Ask what the councillor received in return.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a pattern in appointment data
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-136 sets out the council's appointments and asks the team to read the pattern: of 40 appointments made in the year, 29 went to people recommended by the governing party, 6 went to independent experts, and 5 went to candidates put forward by a professional body.

options.text: The figures show the professional body's candidates were rejected because they lacked political support.
options.misconception: reads a small number as deliberate rejection

options.text: The figures show that party recommendations rarely succeed in competitive recruitment.
options.misconception: ignores the size of the party share of appointments

options.text: The figures show that the appointment process is transparent because each group is represented.
options.misconception: treats representation of groups as evidence of openness

options.text: The figures show a strong party role in appointments, with a substantial professional channel also operating.

questions.explanation: A heavy party share suggests patronage-style appointment, though the professional channel shows the process is not closed. The distractors read a small number as rejection and invert the share.
questions.hint: Read the proportions before judging the process.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a formula-based allocation rule
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-140 asks the team to evaluate a proposal to allocate street repair money using a published formula tied to traffic counts and resident population.

options.text: It is defensible because the rules are public and applied the same way in every neighbourhood.
It is defensible because traffic counts give an objective measure of need in every district.
options.misconception: assumes a measurable proxy is identical to need

options.text: It is defensible because population figures guarantee that no district can be ignored.
options.misconception: assumes equal population guarantees equal treatment

options.text: It is defensible because a formula removes the need for a political decision about priorities.
options.misconception: believes rules substitute for political choice

questions.explanation: A published rule makes allocation transparent and consistently applied. The distractors equate a proxy with need, assume equal population means equal treatment, and deny that rules encode choices.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the rule trustworthy.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Characterise the distributive effect of a levy scheme

stimulus.body: The draft budget raises a levy on properties above a size threshold and uses the revenue to fund a winter fuel payment for low-income households. The note records that 6 per cent of properties are above the threshold, that they hold 41 per cent of assessed housing value, and that the recipients number 22,000 households.

questions.stem: Memo PLAN-144 asks the team to characterise the distributive effect of the scheme described in the note.

options.text: It is mildly redistributive, because a small group of owners pays for a larger group of households.
options.misconception: understates the concentration of housing value

options.text: It is sharply regressive, because the threshold excludes most ordinary household wealth.
options.misconception: assumes thresholds always reach ordinary wealth

options.text: It is clearly redistributive, because a small share of value funds support for a large group of households.
It is neutral, because the number of property owners paying matches the number receiving.
options.misconception: equates equal numbers of parties with equal incidence

questions.explanation: The value pattern and the gap between payers and recipients show resources moving from a narrow group to a broad one. The distractors understate value concentration and assert regressivity.
questions.hint: Compare who pays with who receives.

questions.stem: Memo PLAN-148 asks the team to compute the fine for a food operator who ran twelve days without the required approval at a rate of 250 per day.
questions.explanation: Twelve days at 250 each gives 3,000. The tempting errors apply a discounted rate for early payment, or add a fixed penalty that the memo does not specify.

questions.learningObjective: Challenge a single-cause problem definition
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-152 asks the team to assess the claim that the city's congestion problem is simply a shortage of road space.

options.text: The claim is sound, because congestion always appears where road capacity is lowest.
options.misconception: assumes a single cause explains congestion

options.text: The claim is sound, because widening roads is the standard remedy in every comparable city.
options.misconception: generalises one remedy to all cases

options.text: The claim is sound, because public transport alternatives cannot absorb peak demand.
options.misconception: assumes alternatives can never absorb demand

options.text: The claim is doubtful, because the same congestion may result from timing, pricing and land use.

questions.explanation: Problem definition shapes the remedy, and a single-cause framing narrows options to building more road. The distractors treat one association as one cause and generalise a remedy.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what opened a policy window
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-156 reports that proposals for a parking charge appeared in the forward plan, were deferred three times, and were then adopted within two weeks of a finance report showing the projected revenue was needed to balance next year's budget.

options.text: The window opened when the proposals were first listed in the forward plan.
options.misconception: treats a listing as the moment a window opens

options.text: The window opened when the proposals were deferred for the third time.
options.misconception: treats delay as evidence of a window

options.text: The window opened when the finance report was published, because publicity did the work.
options.misconception: credits publicity alone for the opening

options.text: The window opened when the fiscal need made a previously closed option acceptable.

questions.explanation: Windows open when a policy becomes politically acceptable, often because an external constraint makes it so. The distractors equate listing, delay and publicity with the opening itself.

options.text: Because residents check the restriction themselves and report violations to the council.
options.misconception: assumes voluntary compliance replaces administration

Because a single council committee meets monthly to coordinate every part of the scheme.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Judge a consultation process from its log

stimulus.body: The draft pedestrianisation scheme was circulated to 22 organisations for comment. The remaining 11 organisations, none of which replied, were not contacted again, and the consultation was reported as having broad support.

questions.stem: Memo PLAN-168 asks the team to judge the consultation described in the log.

options.text: The consultation was weak, because the 11 organisations that did not reply were ignored.
options.misconception: treats non-response as evidence of a consultative failure

options.text: The consultation was structured, and the reported support largely reflects the groups that replied.
The consultation was strong, because half of all organisations took the time to respond.
options.misconception: counts replies as a measure of representativeness

options.text: The consultation was weak, because the draft was circulated to a selected list rather than the public.
options.misconception: assumes any closed list undermines a consultation

questions.explanation: Where selected organised bodies shape a draft, apparent support reflects those already engaged. The distractors treat non-response as failure and count replies as representativeness.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the argument that patronage aids responsiveness
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-176 asks the team to evaluate the argument that patronage appointments keep local government responsive.

answer.exemplar: The argument is partly right and partly misleading, and the team should say which part is which. Patronage does keep an administration responsive to the people it governs, because appointees selected for local knowledge know which services are failing, which contractors are reliable and which complaints are honest, and a government that cannot hire or fire its own officers loses a basic management tool. What patronage does not do is test ability or exclude a party that is not prepared to back the government. The defensible position is that some discretionary appointment in the public interest is legitimate and that excessive use, in which loyalty rather than competence decides a post, undermines the very responsiveness it claims to protect, because officials who expect to be removed with the government become cautious rather than effective.

questions.explanation: Patronage can improve local knowledge and administrative control, but excessive use selects for loyalty not competence. The tempting defence misses that the same discretion makes officials cautious.
questions.hint: Ask what the discretion is meant to achieve.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Test a claim that allocation reflects political influence
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-180 asks the team to judge the claim that road repair allocations are simply a reflection of political influence.

options.text: The claim is justified, because allocations differ sharply between areas that vote the same way.
options.misconception: infers influence from any difference between areas

options.text: The claim is justified, because the published formula is applied without any discretion at all.
options.misconception: contradicts the claim while appearing to support it

options.text: The claim is justified, because no technical criterion of need could explain the pattern.
options.misconception: insists only politics can produce any pattern

options.text: The claim is doubtful, because published criteria, applied evenly, would also produce unequal allocations.

questions.explanation: Any rule allocating by need produces unequal spending, so inequality is not evidence of influence. The distractors treat any difference as proof and deny that a criterion could produce a pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what a need-based rule would produce.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State how redistributive policy differs from distributive policy
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-184 asks the team to state what distinguishes redistributive policy from distributive policy.

answer.exemplar: Distributive policy hands benefits out, generally by formula or published criteria, and each recipient gets a share according to rules that apply in the same way to everyone. Redistributive policy changes the distribution itself, moving resources from those who would otherwise receive more towards those who receive less, and it is typically designed so that the pattern of who pays and who gains differs from the existing one. In practice the distinction is a matter of degree rather than kind: a road repair programme may be distributive in form, and a grant that lowers charges in poorer areas is redistributive in effect, because it alters the incidence of costs as well as the level of service. The useful test is therefore whether the policy changes relative positions, not merely whether a formula is used.

questions.explanation: Redistribution changes relative positions, whereas distribution hands out shares under a common rule. The tempting answer rests on the presence of a formula, which both kinds of policy can use.
questions.hint: Ask whether relative positions change.

The rule has worked, because residents now know where to complain and how.
options.misconception: reads more complaints as evidence of compliance

questions.explanation: Regulatory changes raise reporting as well as breach, so complaint data is not a pure measure of the problem. The distractors treat complaints as direct measurement.
questions.hint: Ask what else the rule changed.

options.misconception: reads one inspection as settled political commitment

questions.explanation: Windows close when the resources to act are absent, and a policy with no budget line cannot survive a budget cycle. The distractors credit media pressure with permanence.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain allocations using a published criterion

stimulus.body: The allocation table gives each neighbourhood a share of a 4.2 million pound street fund. options.misconception: assumes population is the only determinant

The allocations are inconsistent, because no single population figure can explain them.
options.misconception: declares the pattern inconsistent without testing it

questions.explanation: Population and a flat supplement both operate, so the larger neighbourhoods are partly offset. The distractors ignore one component or declare inconsistency without testing the stated criterion.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the case for licensing rules
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-228 asks the team to evaluate the argument that licensing rules for street traders reduce the harm they are meant to address.

answer.exemplar: The argument can be true in some circumstances and should not be dismissed, because a rule that is costly to comply with may also reduce the number of traders able to operate, which can shrink the very competition that keeps prices and quality in check. Licensing can also be captured: where a limited number of permits is allocated on the basis of who applies first or who is known, the rule entrenches existing traders and formalises exclusion rather than safety. The defensible position is that the case for licensing rests on genuine safety or amenity objectives, that compliance costs should be proportionate to the harm addressed, and that the evidence for the rule should be tested against what would happen without it, rather than assumed from the existence of complaints.

questions.explanation: The claim deserves testing because compliance costs can restrict supply and entrench incumbents. The tempting dismissal ignores capture and the possibility that licensing shrinks competition.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule does to who can trade.

options.misconception: asserts public acceptance without evidence

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate accountability in a policy web
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-284 asks the team to evaluate the argument that a policy web is a weakness in democratic accountability.

answer.exemplar: The argument identifies a real weakness, and the team should not soften it. A policy subgovernment is a set of actors who sustain a policy through shared routines, and because none of them commands the others, no single body can be asked why a particular decision was taken or who is responsible for a failure. Where the web includes private operators who profit from the policy's continuation, the lack of a clear political owner also makes it harder for the public to identify who should answer for a failure, and it gives organised interests a durable foothold in running the policy. The counter-argument is that demanding a single owner would dissolve the very flexibility that lets a policy adapt to local conditions, so the defensible conclusion is not that webs are harmless but that they require the transparency and reporting that single ownership would otherwise have supplied.

questions.explanation: A web genuinely blurs responsibility, so the argument identifies a real weakness. The tempting counter, that flexibility justifies opacity, concedes the problem without answering it.
questions.hint: Ask who answers for a failure.

options.text: The consultation failed, because accepting most operator proposals indicates capture by the industry.
options.misconception: equates influence with improper capture

questions.explanation: The pattern shows the group with most organisational capacity had the most effect on the rules. The distractors equate access with influence and treat success as capture.
questions.hint: Ask which group could organise a response.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate judging a programme by its reach
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-320 asks the team to evaluate the argument that a programme should be judged on the number of people it reaches.

answer.exemplar: The argument is defensible only if reach is treated as a measure of delivery rather than of effect, and the team should say so plainly. Counting participants tells the council that a service is operating at a given scale, which matters for judging whether a programme is being run as designed and whether the resources committed to it are being used as intended. Reach says nothing, however, about whether the people served are better off: a programme that reaches 6,000 households and changes nothing has delivered a larger output than one that reaches 400 and moves them into stable housing. The defensible conclusion is that reach is a legitimate management measure of output, and an inadequate measure of outcome, so a programme judged on reach alone will be rewarded for size rather than effect and will eventually be cheapest to inflate.

questions.explanation: Reach measures delivery, not effect, so it is legitimate for management but inadequate as an outcome measure. The tempting claim mistakes scale for benefit and rewards inflation.
questions.hint: Ask what changed for the people counted.

questions.learningObjective: Name the defining feature of a policy web
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-324 describes a waste collection round that continued through a change of contractor because the crews, the depot supervisor and the software supplier all followed the same routine, and asks the team to name the feature this illustrates.

options.text: A policy sustained by a network of actors with no single body in control.
A policy sustained by a single department with firm central oversight.
options.misconception: mistakes a network for central control

options.text: A policy sustained by the strength of a written service contract.

questions.explanation: Persistence without a controlling authority is the defining feature of a policy subgovernment. The distractors substitute central oversight, a contract and one individual's effort.
questions.hint: Ask who could have stopped the round.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why organised groups receive privileged access
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-328 asks the team to explain why organised business groups are often given privileged access to consultation.

options.text: Because business groups are more consistent in their submissions than other groups are.
options.misconception: attributes access to submission quality alone

options.text: Because the law requires every policy to be consulted on by a single designated body.
options.misconception: invents a statutory consultation requirement

options.text: Because their members' interests are directly affected, so consultation is efficient for all.
Because other groups are consulted through the same channel at other times.
options.misconception: assumes access is a matter of scheduling

questions.explanation: Privileged access reflects organised interests' stake in the outcome and their ability to represent a position coherently. The distractors attribute it to submission quality and to a statutory rule.
questions.hint: Ask what makes their advice efficient.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh audit evidence of clientelist exchange

stimulus.body: The audit found that 62 of the 340 small grants awarded in the year went to households in the two wards where the governing councillor had the smallest margin, and that 41 of those 62 recipients were listed as supporters in the councillor's published register of interests. Grants in other wards were distributed through an open panel with published scoring, and 28 of the 340 grants had been decided that way.

questions.stem: Memo PLAN-332 asks the team to weigh what the audit finding shows about clientelism in the two wards.

options.text: The finding proves the councillor took bribes, because the grants went to supporters.
options.misconception: jumps from a pattern to a criminal conclusion

options.text: The concentration and the register together are consistent with a political exchange.
The finding proves the grants were objectively unjustified, because open scoring always works.
options.misconception: assumes a procedural alternative guarantees better decisions

options.text: The finding shows nothing, because 62 grants out of 340 is a small number overall.
options.misconception: dismisses a concentrated pattern by the overall total

questions.explanation: The concentration in two wards and the overlap with the supporter register fit an exchange between discretion and support. The distractors jump to bribery and dismiss the pattern.
questions.hint: Ask what the pattern and the register share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the average length of service of appointees
questions.stem: Memo PLAN-336 asks the team to work out the average length of service in months for a set of 54 appointees who served 486 months in total.
questions.explanation: 486 months divided by 54 appointees gives an average of 9 months. The tempting error divides by 12, confusing appointments with years, and another converts months to years first.
questions.hint: Divide total months by the number of appointees.
